strengths: Introduces a novel, purpose-built dataset (WHOOPS-AHA!) for mechanistic study of cross-modal knowledge conflict in VLMs, filling a clear gap since prior multimodal conflict work is largely behavioral/black-box.

Extends the logit-lens/mechanistic interpretability framework of Ortu et al. (2024) from text-only LLMs to the multimodal setting, showing a clean functional dissociation between attention (favoring counterfactual/visual info) and MLP blocks (favoring factual/internal knowledge), consistent with prior findings on MLPs as knowledge stores.

Localizes a small set of attention heads that mediate the conflict and demonstrates strong causal control via targeted, bidirectional multiplicative interventions, with large and consistent swings in factual accuracy (e.g., 22%→74% for LLaVA-NeXT, 18%→83% for Gemma3), including a random-head control that shows specificity of the effect.

The attention-based attribution method for localizing conflict-inducing image patches is shown to outperform gradient-based saliency in a well-designed pixel-ablation experiment, with both quantitative (accuracy vs. % pixels removed, random baseline control) and qualitative (patch visualization) evidence.

Findings are replicated across two architecturally different VLMs (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3), improving generality; reasonable ablations are provided (number of heads, KL-divergence for generation quality, random head/patch controls).

Clear writing, good related-work positioning including timely discussion of concurrent work (Golovanevsky et al. 2025a), and reasonable reproducibility details (compute, code/dataset release, licensing).
weaknesses: Dataset scale is small (500 base images, ~430 filtered examples per model) and construction relies heavily on GPT-4o generation with only manual verification described minimally; no inter-annotator agreement, filtering criteria details, or dataset statistics (e.g., token diversity, category distribution) are given, limiting confidence in dataset quality and generality.

The core method (logit lens, single representative token per example, last-token-position analysis) is acknowledged as an approximation; using only one factual/counterfactual token per example is a significant simplification of the generative process and may not fully capture real generation dynamics.

Interventions and analyses are restricted to the final token position and to attention heads only, ignoring potential contributions of MLPs, the vision encoder, or earlier token positions in a more causal/thorough manner (though this is disclosed as a limitation).

The claim that attention-based attribution 'outperforms' gradient-based attribution is based on a single downstream proxy (factual-accuracy shift under ablation) rather than a ground-truth localization benchmark (e.g., human-annotated regions), which could bias the comparison toward the proposed method since it was derived from the same heads used to define the intervention groups.

Results are demonstrated on only two mid-sized VLMs; it's unclear how well findings generalize to larger or differently architected models (e.g., different vision-language fusion mechanisms), limiting the scope of the claimed generality.

The generation-quality analysis (KL divergence, qualitative captioning examples) is fairly cursory and only reported for LLaVA-NeXT, not systematically for both models, weakening claims about the practical usability of the steering intervention.

The paper's contribution is primarily analytical/diagnostic (as acknowledged in Discussion), with no proposed mitigation method or robustness improvement, somewhat limiting its immediate practical impact despite being clearly stated as out of scope.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored problem: the internal mechanisms by which VLMs arbitrate between parametric knowledge and visual context, extending the 'competition of mechanisms' framework from unimodal LMs (Ortu et al., 2024) into the multimodal setting.

The empirical narrative is built from multiple converging lines of evidence rather than a single analysis: logit-lens localization (block- and head-level), causal attention-head intervention, and attention-based visual attribution with ablation — all cross-validated with sensible control experiments (random heads, random pixels).
Findings are replicated across two architecturally distinct models (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3), and the qualitative attribution patterns (Fig. 6) are intuitive and interpretable.

The paper is transparent about limitations of the Logit Lens and about restricting analysis to the final token position, and reports quantitative checks (rank shift, KL divergence) to justify the intervention strength range used.
Code/dataset release and a reasonably detailed reproducibility section (compute, libraries, license) support replication.
weaknesses: The dataset is small (500 WHOOPS! images, filtered to ~430-436 usable examples per model), and the manual verification process for GPT-4o–generated factual/counterfactual token sets is not described in enough detail (number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, criteria) to assess dataset quality or reproducibility of the labeling.

The core mechanistic claims rest heavily on Logit Lens, a technique known to introduce distortions from non-final residual projections; the paper acknowledges this but does not attempt a more robust alternative (e.g., tuned lens) or otherwise control for the confound that late-layer bias in Logit Lens outputs could itself explain the localization to final layers.

Analysis and intervention are restricted to a single representative token pair per example at the final prompt position, which is a coarse proxy for the full generative process; the authors acknowledge this but it limits the strength of claims about how conflicts are resolved during actual generation.

The choice of exactly 20 heads for the intervention/attribution experiments is justified somewhat post hoc ('optimal balance'), without a principled selection criterion, raising concern about cherry-picking of the effective head set.

Overlap with concurrent work (Golovanevsky et al., 2025a) on steering vectors for modality competition is substantial in spirit (identifying/manipulating components that control visual vs. parametric reliance); the paper's differentiation is described mainly in terms of dataset design (complex scenes vs. simple attribute edits) rather than methodological novelty, weakening the claim of a clearly distinct contribution.

Qualitative visual grounding results (Fig. 6) are presented with only two hand-picked examples; no systematic human evaluation or larger-scale qualitative analysis is provided to substantiate the claim that attention attribution is semantically meaningful beyond the aggregate ablation curves.

The intervention itself is a simple multiplicative reweighting of attention at the last token, without comparison to alternative causal methods (e.g., activation patching, head ablation, mean-ablation baselines) that are standard in the mechanistic interpretability literature, limiting confidence that this is the most rigorous or informative intervention choice.

The contribution remains primarily diagnostic; the paper does not propose or evaluate any practical mitigation strategy building on the localized heads, somewhat limiting its broader applied impact despite claims of relevance to 'developing more interpretable and controllable systems.'

strengths: Introduces WHOOPS-AHA!, a carefully constructed dataset that operationalizes multimodal knowledge conflict in a controlled way, extending the WHOOPS! benchmark with paired factual/counterfactual continuations verified via a two-stage GPT-4o generation + manual filtering process.

Provides a coherent, multi-pronged mechanistic analysis: logit-lens localization at both the block level (attention vs. MLP) and individual head level, followed by causal validation through targeted attention-weight interventions, which is methodologically stronger than purely correlational interpretability work.
Includes appropriate control experiments (random head interventions, random pixel ablations) that isolate the specificity of the identified components, strengthening the causal claims.

Results are replicated across two architecturally distinct VLMs (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3), lending some generality to the localization findings (attention favors counterfactual, MLP favors factual; conflict resolved in late layers).

The attention-based attribution for visual patches is compared quantitatively (ablation curves) and qualitatively (illustrative examples) against gradient-based attribution, with a fairly convincing demonstration of superior precision.
Reasonable reproducibility support: compute budget stated, public model/library usage, dataset license noted, and full prompts for dataset construction included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The dataset is fairly small (~430–436 examples per model) since it is derived from the 500-image WHOOPS! collection, and per-example evaluation collapses the generative distribution into a single representative factual/counterfactual token pair, which the authors acknowledge as a simplification but that limits how well findings generalize to fuller, free-form generation.

Only two models are evaluated; while they differ in family, this is a narrow basis for claims about general VLM behavior, and no larger or more diverse model set (e.g., different scales within a family) is tested to assess how consistent the localized-head phenomenon is.

Heavy reliance on Logit Lens, which is explicitly noted to introduce distortions from non-final residual projections; no comparison with more robust alternatives (e.g., Tuned Lens) is attempted to validate the localization findings.

The selection of 20 heads per group is justified with a supporting appendix curve but still appears somewhat heuristic, and the paper does not explore sensitivity of causal/attribution results to this choice beyond one ablation figure.

The mechanistic scope is restricted to attention heads at the final token position; potential contributions from MLPs, earlier token positions, or the visual encoder to conflict resolution are not explored, despite MLPs being shown to matter in the block-level analysis.

The counterfactual scenario (visually absurd WHOOPS!-style images) is a narrow and somewhat artificial instantiation of "knowledge conflict"; it's unclear how well the identified heads/mechanisms transfer to more naturalistic or adversarial conflict settings (e.g., outdated facts, deceptive images) mentioned in the introduction as motivating cases.

No human/automatic quality control metrics are reported for the GPT-4o-generated factual/counterfactual token sets beyond "manual verification," leaving some uncertainty about annotation reliability and potential GPT-4o biases baked into the dataset.

strengths: Introduces a well-constructed dataset (WHOOPS-AHA!) with a clear, controlled setup for inducing verifiable knowledge conflicts, accompanied by substantial quality-control efforts (LLM-as-judge across two independent judges plus human validation with agreement statistics).

Methodology is rigorous and includes multiple complementary lines of evidence: logit-lens localization, causal attention-head interventions, and attention/gradient-based visual attribution with quantitative overlap metrics against segmented ground truth (SAM-based), lending convergent support to the central claims.

Strong control experiments strengthen causal claims: random-head intervention baseline, MLP-intervention baseline showing weaker effects, and a POPE specificity test showing the identified heads are not generically vision-related but specifically recruited under conflict.

Findings are replicated across two distinct VLM architectures (LLaVA-NeXT and Gemma3) and generalize to an independently constructed dataset (Visual CounterFact) with substantial overlap in identified heads, suggesting the discovered mechanism is not an artifact of a single dataset or model.

The paper is transparent about limitations (logit-lens approximation errors, single-token simplification, late-fusion-only scope) and provides extensive reproducibility details (compute, code/dataset release, prompts, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses including KL-divergence checks for intervention strength).
weaknesses: The quantitative visual-attribution comparison (Average Ratio vs. gradient/random baselines) is based on only 20 sampled images, which is a fairly small sample for the statistical claims being made, even though appropriate given manual segmentation costs.

Analysis is restricted to two late-fusion, LLaVA-style architectures; while the paper acknowledges this and shows some generalization, the applicability to other VLM families (early/mid-fusion, larger models) remains untested.

Reliance on a single representative factual/counterfactual token per example (rather than full generative behavior) simplifies the phenomenon and may not fully capture how conflicts manifest in free-form generation, a limitation the authors note but do not empirically address.

Human validation of the LLM-as-judge dataset construction shows only moderate exact agreement (35–70%) on several dimensions, raising some concern about the precision of automatic quality filtering, though adjacent-agreement rates are high.

The core conceptual contribution (attention vs. MLP functional dissociation in factual/contextual conflict, and identifiable head-level competition) extends findings already established in text-only LLMs (e.g., Ortu et al. 2024) to the multimodal setting; the novelty is more incremental synthesis/extension than a fundamentally new mechanism, though the specific multimodal localization and visual-attribution results are valuable additions.
